title: The Agilometer
blurb: Explain what the Agilometer assesses, recognise its sliders, and say where it is assessed and reviewed.
question: A project board wants a regular view of how risky agile working is on its project, area by area. Which tool helps, and in which workshop is it reviewed?

teach.h: A risk tool for agile working itself
teach.body: The Agilometer is a tool to identify and monitor the risks of agile working. It defines six areas where adopting agile could cause problems if left unmanaged, and each area is graded on a scale from low to high for its agile suitability. In plain terms: it asks how ready this environment is for agile, slider by slider, so weak spots are seen early. It is an artifact of the risk practice, alongside the risk management approach and the risk register.

teach.h: The sliders and what high looks like
head: Slider
At the high end
rows: Stakeholders happy to flex scope and prioritize
Benefit delivered by regular partial releases
Supportive setting, contracts that allow agile
teach.caption: Five of the six sliders named in 10.3.2.2. 'Iterative and incremental' is short for 'ability to work iteratively and deliver incrementally'.

teach.h: Read each slider for what it tells you
teach.body: Each slider points to a different kind of risk. A low reading on flexibility means stakeholders resist flexing what is delivered; a low reading on environmental conditions may mean a contract that blocks agile ways of working. The value lies in seeing which area is weak and acting on it. A slider can be raised: for flexibility, the book suggests challenging whether too many requirements are Must haves, or the assumptions behind them.

In directing a project, the agile enablement workshop holds regular Agilometer assessments in initiation and later stages, so agile maturity and agile risks are reviewed again and again. It brings together the project board, agile coaches and organizational or business representatives. Its topics are: Agilometer assessment review, risk identification (extra agile-adoption threats and opportunities), risk assessment (probability, impact, priority) and risk planning (practical mitigation steps).

teach.h: Example reading: Fenwick Water first assessment
teach.caption: Illustrative readings for the scenario below; not figures from the book.

teach.body: At Fenwick Water, project manager Tomasz Nowak runs the project initiation workshop for a new customer app. Everyone rates each slider; the views are combined into one project Agilometer. Flexibility is low because the sponsor has labelled almost every feature a Must have, and environmental conditions are low because the supplier contract fixes a full specification. Tomasz records both as risks. At the agile enablement workshop, executive Ruth Okafor and agile coach Dev Mistry plan mitigations and agree to reassess next stage.

teach.text: The Agilometer belongs to the RISK practice and assesses the risks of agile working. It is not a progress chart, not a quality check and not a way to decide whether a change request alters the baseline.

items: Purpose: identify and monitor the risks of agile working (10.3.1).
Six areas, each graded low to high for agile suitability.
Sliders include flexibility on what is delivered, level of collaboration, ease of communication, ability to work iteratively and deliver incrementally, advantageous environmental conditions.
Raise flexibility by challenging too many Must haves (10.3.2.3).
First combined assessment: project initiation workshop. Regular reassessment: agile enablement workshop in directing a project.

summary: You can now explain that the Agilometer is a risk-practice tool for the risks of agile working, graded low to high across six areas. You can also recognise its sliders and say that it is first assessed in the project initiation workshop and regularly reviewed in the agile enablement workshop.

A.q: What is the Agilometer used for?
options: To track story points completed in each iteration
To identify and monitor the risks of agile working
To decide whether a change affects the baseline
To record the status and history of each risk
A.why: The Agilometer is a tool to identify and monitor the risks of agile working (10.3.1).

whyNot.0: Tracking completed points is done with burn charts and velocity in the progress practice.
whyNot.2: Deciding baseline versus detail change is part of the issues practice.
whyNot.3: The status and history of individual risks are held in the risk register.

A.q: To which practice does the Agilometer belong in PRINCE2 Agile V2?
A.why: The Agilometer is an artifact of the risk practice, alongside the risk management approach and the risk register (10.3.2, Table 10.1).

whyNot.0: The quality practice covers requirements, acceptance criteria and the DoD, not the Agilometer.
whyNot.1: The progress practice uses burn charts and dashboards; the Agilometer can show trends there but belongs to risk.
whyNot.2: The plans practice covers the release map and backlogs, not the Agilometer.

A.q: Which Agilometer slider covers a working environment, including contracts, that supports agile working?
options: Ability to work iteratively and deliver incrementally
A.why: Advantageous environmental conditions looks at whether the overall environment supports agile, including contracts that do not inhibit it (10.3.2.2).

whyNot.1: This slider concerns delivering benefit through regular partial releases, not the wider setting or contracts.
whyNot.2: Flexibility on what is delivered concerns stakeholder comfort with flexing scope and prioritizing.
whyNot.3: Ease of communication concerns how easily all parties can communicate.

B.q: Which workshop, in the directing a project process, holds regular Agilometer assessments?
B.why: The agile enablement workshop holds regular Agilometer assessments in initiation and later stages so agile risks are reviewed regularly (Table 13.5).

whyNot.0: The project initiation workshop first combines everyone's Agilometer views, but it belongs to initiating a project.
whyNot.1: The progress review workshop is in controlling a stage and reviews status and current risks and issues.
whyNot.3: The team retrospective is in managing product delivery and covers the good, the bad, the learning and team building.

B.q: Stakeholders insist that nearly every requirement is a Must have. Which slider would challenging those priorities help to raise?
B.why: The book suggests raising flexibility on what is delivered by challenging whether too many requirements are Must haves (10.3.2.3).

whyNot.0: Ease of communication concerns how easily parties talk, not how requirements are prioritized.
whyNot.2: Working together may help collaboration, but challenging Musts targets flexibility on what is delivered.
whyNot.3: Environmental conditions concern the wider setting and contracts, not the priority of requirements.

B.q:
Which two statements about the Agilometer are correct?
1. Each area is graded from low to high for agile suitability.
2. It is used to decide whether a request for change needs the board.
3. In the project initiation workshop, individual assessments are combined into one.
4. It replaces burn charts for reporting progress to the board.
B.why: Areas are graded low to high for agile suitability (1), and the project initiation workshop combines everyone's assessments into one project Agilometer (3) (10.3.1, Table 13.7).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: baseline decisions belong to the issues practice, not the Agilometer.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: the Agilometer neither decides change requests nor replaces burn charts.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: burn charts remain the progress tool; the Agilometer is a risk tool.

C.q: Who takes part in the agile enablement workshop, and what does it do with the Agilometer?
options: Board, agile coaches and business reps; reassess it
Delivery team and team coach; set iteration goals
Project manager and project support; publish it weekly
Chief product owner and product owners; rank the backlog
C.why: The agile enablement workshop is for the project board, agile coaches and organizational or business representatives, and reassesses the Agilometer regularly (Table 13.5).

whyNot.1: Setting iteration goals with the team is the team planning workshop in managing product delivery.
whyNot.2: Project support may help with dashboards, but the workshop is a board-level event with agile coaches.
whyNot.3: Backlog ranking is the work of the CPO and POs, not the purpose of this workshop.

C.q: In which workshop are all participants' Agilometer views first combined, and in which process does it sit?
options: Project canvas workshop; starting up a project
Agile enablement workshop; directing a project
Release planning workshop; managing a stage boundary
Project initiation workshop; initiating a project
C.why: The Agilometer is a topic of the project initiation workshop, where all participants assess it and the results are combined into one; the workshop belongs to initiating a project (Table 13.7).

whyNot.0: The project canvas workshop builds the canvas in starting up; it does not combine Agilometer views.
whyNot.1: The agile enablement workshop reassesses the Agilometer regularly; the first combined assessment is in initiation.
whyNot.2: The release planning workshop covers OKRs and the release map, not the Agilometer.

C.q: A client can accept the new system only as one complete delivery at the end, with no partial releases. Which slider is likely to read low?
options: The iterative and incremental delivery slider
The flexibility on what is delivered slider
C.why: The full name is ability to work iteratively and deliver incrementally. At the high end, benefit is easily delivered through regular partial deliveries, so a single end delivery points to a low reading (10.3.2.2).

whyNot.0: Collaboration concerns how closely people work together, not how the product is released.
whyNot.2: Environmental conditions concern the wider setting and contracts; the problem here is the lack of partial releases.
whyNot.3: Flexibility concerns comfort with flexing scope; the issue here is partial delivery.

reteach.title: A pre-flight checklist for agile
reteach.question: If agile working were an aircraft, what would the Agilometer be?

blocks.h: Gauges before take-off, and during the flight
blocks.body: Pilots check each gauge before take-off and keep watching them in the air. One reading in the red is enough to act on, whatever the others say. The Agilometer works the same way: each slider is a gauge for one kind of agile risk. The team reads them first in the project initiation workshop, and the board keeps checking them in the agile enablement workshop.

rows.label: Topic
values: Is this setting ready for agile?
Is this change a baseline change?

blocks.text: First combined assessment: project initiation workshop. Regular board review: agile enablement workshop. Both are about agile risk, not progress.

explain.body: The Agilometer identifies and monitors the risks of agile working. It defines six areas, each graded low to high for agile suitability.

test.q: How is each Agilometer area graded?
options: From low to high for agile suitability
As a probability multiplied by impact
As red, amber or green for progress
In story points for each iteration
test.why: Each of the six areas is graded on a scale from low to high according to its agile suitability (10.3.1).

whyNot.1: Probability and impact are used when assessing individual risks, not to grade Agilometer areas.
whyNot.2: RAG status is a progress reporting style, not the Agilometer scale.
whyNot.3: Story points measure effort for estimation and velocity.

explain.body: Named sliders include flexibility on what is delivered, level of collaboration, ease of communication, ability to work iteratively and deliver incrementally, and advantageous environmental conditions.

test.q: Which slider concerns how comfortable stakeholders are with flexing scope and their role in prioritizing?
test.why: Flexibility on what is delivered looks at stakeholder comfort with flexing scope and with their part in prioritizing work (10.3.2.2).

whyNot.0: Ease of communication concerns how easily all parties communicate.
whyNot.1: Environmental conditions concern the wider setting, including contracts.
whyNot.2: Level of collaboration concerns how closely people work together.

explain.body: All participants assess it in the project initiation workshop, combined into one. The board, agile coaches and business representatives reassess it regularly in the agile enablement workshop.

test.q: Which of these is a topic of the agile enablement workshop?
test.why: The agile enablement workshop topics are Agilometer assessment review, risk identification, risk assessment and risk planning (Table 13.5).

whyNot.0: Backlog refinement is a topic of the team planning workshop.
whyNot.2: OKR definition is a topic of the release planning workshop.
whyNot.3: The team skill matrix is a topic of the project kickoff workshop.

explain.body: Sliders can be improved. For flexibility on what is delivered, challenge whether too many requirements are Must haves, or the assumptions behind them.

test.q: Which action does the book suggest for improving the flexibility on what is delivered slider?
options: Moving the whole team into one shared office space
Rewriting the supplier contract to allow agile terms
Challenging whether too many items are Must haves
Adding an extra iteration to each release
test.why: Challenging whether too many requirements are Must haves, or their assumptions, can raise flexibility on what is delivered (10.3.2.3).

whyNot.0: Co-location may help collaboration or communication, not flexibility on scope.
whyNot.1: Contract terms relate to advantageous environmental conditions.
whyNot.3: Adding iterations changes the plan; it does not make stakeholders more flexible on scope.
